h1:
10 Best Khao Soi Shops
in Chiang Mai
intro: Khao soi is the first dish most people picture when they think of Chiang Mai: egg noodles in a coconut-curry broth made with northern spices, topped with crispy fried noodles, and eaten with pickled mustard greens, shallots, and lime. But search around and you'll turn up hundreds of shops, so we've narrowed it down to 10 you won't regret ordering at. The mix runs from legendary old-timers that have been around for decades, to Michelin Guide listings, to a new-generation shop in Nimman. We work through them one neighbourhood at a time, in town and around the edges, with the standout bowls, the price per bowl, and the opening hours laid out plainly.

blocks.html: First, a quick word on what actually makes one bowl of khao soi better than another. It all comes down to the broth. Some shops go for a thick, spice-forward curry; others lean sweeter and milder on the coconut milk, which is easier to drink. The heat level varies a lot from shop to shop too. The noodles and the sides are much the same everywhere, so the broth and the meat are really what you're judging. We've grouped the list to make it easy to choose: legendary old-timers, in-town shops that are easy to reach, out-of-town spots you'll need a car for, and the new generation, so you can pick by whichever zone you're staying in that day.

blocks.title: How to read this list
blocks.html: The order here isn't a ranking of winners and losers. Khao soi is pure personal taste, and someone who likes a thick, intense broth will land on a different shop than someone who likes it mild and creamy. So we spell out what each shop does best, to help you pick the one that suits your own palate rather than just following the hype.

blocks.text: The legendary old-timers around Fa Ham

blocks.html: The Fa Ham area along the Ping River is Chiang Mai's old khao soi heartland. Several legendary shops cluster around Charoenrat Road near Wat Fa Ham, and locals have been eating here since childhood. If you want to taste the original style that's been part of the city for decades, this is where to start. It gets very busy around lunchtime, so leave some extra time to find parking.

items.name: Khao Soi Lamduan Fa Ham
items.blurb: The legendary khao soi shop that's part of Chiang Mai itself, open since around 1943 — more than 80 years — and a Michelin Guide listing. The broth is rich and fragrant with spices, well-balanced and not too spicy: an original-style bowl that many people use as the benchmark for everywhere else. Prices are friendly. The queue is long at lunch and parking is hard to find, so we'd come mid-morning or in the early afternoon.
items.meta: Charoenrat Road, Fa Ham · open roughly 08:30–16:30 daily

items.name: Khao Soi Samoejai Fa Ham
items.blurb: Another old-timer right beside Wat Fa Ham, in the same pocket as Lamduan, open for more than 30 years. The broth is rich and the braised chicken and beef are nicely tender. What we like is that you can add northern dishes like nam ngiao, sai ua, and khao kan jin to the same meal. Chiang Mai locals love arguing over whether Lamduan or Samoejai is better — they're very close together, so try both and decide for yourself.
items.meta: Charoenrat Road, beside Wat Fa Ham · open roughly 08:00–17:00

blocks.title: A tip for the Fa Ham side
blocks.html: These two shops are only a few steps apart, so if there are several of you, split your order between them and taste them side by side in one trip. Traffic is heavy around lunchtime, so if you're staying in the Old City, taking a Grab or a songthaew (red truck) is easier than driving yourself.

blocks.text: In-town shops that are easy to reach

blocks.html: If you'd rather not drive far, there's plenty of great khao soi right in town — around Nimman, the Old City, and Charoen Prathet near the Night Bazaar. This group suits anyone staying in the centre who wants to walk or grab a quick ride without losing time heading out of town.

items.name: Khao Soi Mae Sai (Ratchaphruek, Chang Phueak)
items.blurb: An old-timer that both locals and international reviewers single out as often as anywhere, and a Michelin Guide listing. The broth is nicely balanced — fragrant with coconut milk but not cloying, with just the right heat — the braised beef falls apart, and the noodles have a good chew. The standout quality is that everything is good, with no weak point. It's in the Chang Phueak area, an easy walk from Nimman, and it makes a great first stop if you've just arrived in Chiang Mai.
items.meta: Ratchaphruek Road, Chang Phueak, near Nimman · open morning–afternoon

items.name: Khao Soi Khun Yai (Old City, Soi Si Phum)
items.blurb: A shop down a small lane in the Old City that plenty of Chiang Mai locals call their favourite. The chicken khao soi really shines — the broth and noodles work together beautifully — and the vibe is homey and relaxed, with friendly prices. The catch is the short hours and that it usually sells out fast, so if you've got your heart set on this one, go before noon.
items.meta: Old City, Soi Si Phum · open morning to around noon, closed Sundays

items.name: Khao Soi Islam (Charoen Prathet)
items.blurb: A Muslim / Chin Haw khao soi shop beside the Ban Haw Mosque in the Charoen Prathet area near the Night Bazaar, part of this neighbourhood for more than 40 years. It's halal khao soi: the broth is fragrant with spices, the noodles are house-made, and the flavour isn't overpowering. The chicken and braised-beef bowls are the highlights, and there's khao mok (Thai biryani), oxtail soup, and salad khaek to order alongside. The taste is clearly different from the usual coconut-style khao soi.
items.meta: Soi 1, Charoen Prathet Road, near the Night Bazaar · open roughly 08:00–17:00

items.name: Khao Soi Sriphan (Nong Hoi)
items.blurb: A long-running old shop in the Nong Hoi area serving khao soi and nam ngiao in a local style, with a choice of chicken, pork, beef, and meatballs. The noodles have a good chew, topped with crispy noodles, and the broth is well-balanced and rich without being too intense. It's a good pick if you want a middle-of-the-road khao soi that's easy to eat, and you can try nam ngiao in the same place.
items.meta: Ko Klang Road, Nong Hoi · open roughly 08:00–16:00, closed Wednesdays

blocks.title: Halal or vegetarian
blocks.html: If you're after halal khao soi, Khao Soi Islam in the Charoen Prathet area is the main choice. For vegetarian or vegan eaters, Chiang Mai has several shops doing vegetarian/vegan khao soi around Nimman and the Old City — see our Chiang Mai vegetarian food guide for more.

If you have a car and don't mind driving, several out-of-town shops are worth the petrol. A few are famous enough that people drive out of the city just to eat there, and they make a good stop if you're already heading out toward Mae Rim, San Kamphaeng, or San Sai.

items.name: Khao Soi Lung Prakit Kad Kom (the "Netflix khao soi")
items.blurb: A shop in Kad Kom market south of the Old City that took off after appearing on international media — people now call it the "Netflix khao soi" — and it's held a Michelin Guide listing several years running. The draw is the braised-beef khao soi: meltingly tender meat with soft tendon, in a rich broth fragrant with condensed milk. It's good value for the portion. Locals and tourists mix here, and it sells out fast in the afternoon.
items.meta: Suriyawong Road, Kad Kom market, south of the Old City · open roughly 09:30–16:30

items.name: Khao Soi Mae Manee (Chang Phueak, on the way to Mae Rim)
items.blurb: An old-timer down a lane around Chang Phueak on the way up to Mae Rim, still cooking over a traditional charcoal stove, with a Michelin Guide listing three years running. The broth is rich, bold, and fragrant with spices, and the braised beef-shank khao soi has a springy, chewy bite. Anyone who likes an intense broth will be very happy here. It's a good stop on the way to Mon Cham or Mae Rim — you just have to head a little way into the lane.
items.meta: Soi 24, Chotana Road, Chang Phueak · open roughly 09:00–15:30, closed on Buddhist holy days

items.name: Khao Soi Lung Pan (San Kamphaeng)
items.blurb: A genuinely northern khao soi shop out around San Kamphaeng, near the Bo Sang road, open for many years. The broth uses thin coconut milk — not heavy and split with oil, but fragrant with a traditional curry-paste recipe. The standouts are the local free-range chicken khao soi, with firm, tender meat, and the beef-shank khao soi with its slightly crunchy tendon. There's noodle soup and pork satay to order too, making it a good stop when you're out exploring San Kamphaeng.
items.meta: Bo Sang Road, San Kamphaeng · open roughly 08:30–14:30

blocks.label: Half-day trip
blocks.title: A khao soi hunt north of the city

items.activity: Start at Khao Soi Mae Sai in Chang Phueak
items.note: Come early before it fills up, and taste it as your baseline first

items.activity: Drive up to Khao Soi Mae Manee on Chotana Road
items.note: If you like an intense broth, you can compare it against Mae Sai

items.activity: Loop back to Fa Ham — Lamduan or Samoejai by the Ping
items.note: Finish with the original style; leave time to find parking

items.activity: Sit down for coffee at a riverside café to recover
items.note: Three bowls of khao soi in — time for a break

blocks.html: Beyond the old-timers, Chiang Mai also has newer shops that serve khao soi in a relaxed café or sit-down northern-restaurant setting. They suit anyone who wants their khao soi with a nice photo, or a full northern spread in one meal. Prices run a bit higher than the roadside shops, but you're trading up for the atmosphere and comfortable seating.

items.name: Khao Soi Nimman (Nimmanhaemin Soi 13)
items.blurb: A khao soi shop in Nimman with a Michelin Guide listing that stays open late — handy if you're staying around Nimman and want khao soi in the evening or at night, which is hard to find at the old-timers. The broth is fragrant with coconut milk and well-balanced, the room is clean and comfortable, and it's the most convenient option if you don't want to head far out.
items.meta: Nimmanhaemin Soi 13 · open late into the evening

blocks.html: If you'd like your khao soi as part of a full northern spread, well-known northern restaurants like Tong Tem Toh in a Nimman soi or Huen Muan Jai around Chang Phueak also do a solid khao soi at restaurant level. They're great to visit as a group and order nam phrik ong, sai ua, and kaeng hang le to share. We've written about these places in full in our Chiang Mai northern food guide — follow along there to read more.

blocks.text: How to pick the right shop for your taste

items.name: You like a thick, spice-fragrant broth
items.blurb: Lamduan and Samoejai in Fa Ham, or Mae Manee out toward Chang Phueak — heavy broth, fragrant with spices.

items.name: You like it mild and easy
items.blurb: Mae Sai in Chang Phueak, Khun Yai in the Old City, or Nimman — well-balanced and easy to eat.

items.name: You want a halal / Chin Haw flavour
items.blurb: Khao Soi Islam in the Charoen Prathet area — fragrant with spices, not heavy on coconut, with khao mok.

items.name: You're after a hearty braised-beef bowl
items.blurb: Lung Prakit at Kad Kom, the "Netflix khao soi" — meltingly tender beef in a rich broth.

blocks.title: Chicken or beef — which to start with
blocks.html: If you've never had it, start with the chicken khao soi: the flavour is more middle-of-the-road and familiar. The beef version is more heavily braised and more fragrant with spices. The shops known for their beef are Lamduan, Islam, and Lung Prakit at Kad Kom.

blocks.text: Prices, hours, and things to know

items: Price per bowl — most roadside khao soi shops run about 40–60 THB, while shops in Nimman or sit-down northern restaurants are 60–70 THB and up.

Hours — many old-timers open morning to afternoon (roughly 08:00–16:30) and often sell out before closing. If you've got a famous shop in mind, go before noon; if you want khao soi in the evening or at night, choose a Nimman shop.
Closing days — some shops have a fixed day off: Khun Yai is closed Sundays, Sriphan on Wednesdays, Mae Manee on Buddhist holy days. Check before you set out to be sure.
Cash — many small shops take cash or PromptPay, so carrying small notes makes things easier.
Sides — pickled mustard greens, shallots, and lime are on the table; a squeeze of lime and some pickles cut through the richness of the coconut broth nicely.
Parking — the Fa Ham and Kad Kom areas get jammed around lunch, so leave time to find a spot, or take a Grab to make it easier.

faq.q: Which khao soi shop in Chiang Mai is the safe bet that won't disappoint?
faq.a: If you want the original style, the Fa Ham old-timers like Khao Soi Lamduan and Samoejai are the main choices. For something easy to reach in town, go for Khao Soi Mae Sai in Chang Phueak and Khao Soi Khun Yai in the Old City. For a first stop, Mae Sai and Lamduan are hard to get wrong — both are Michelin Guide listings.

faq.q: Which khao soi shops in Chiang Mai are in the Michelin Guide?
faq.a: Several shops on this list are recommended in the Michelin Guide, including Khao Soi Lamduan Fa Ham, Khao Soi Mae Sai, Khao Soi Lung Prakit at Kad Kom, Khao Soi Mae Manee, and Khao Soi Nimman. All are genuinely open and popular with locals.

faq.q: How much is a bowl of khao soi in Chiang Mai?
faq.a: Ordinary roadside khao soi shops run about 40–60 THB a bowl, while shops in Nimman or sit-down northern restaurants are around 60–70 THB and up. That price already includes the table sides — pickles, shallots, and lime.

faq.q: When should I go for khao soi, and are any shops open in the evening?
faq.a: Many old-timers open morning to afternoon (roughly 08:00–16:30) and sell out fast, so we'd aim for breakfast through to before noon. If you want khao soi in the evening or at night, choose a Nimman shop like Khao Soi Nimman, which stays open late.

faq.q: Is there a halal khao soi shop in Chiang Mai?
faq.a: Yes — Khao Soi Islam in the Charoen Prathet Road area, beside the Ban Haw Mosque near the Night Bazaar, is a Chin Haw-style halal shop that's been around for more than 40 years. The chicken and beef bowls are the highlights, the noodles are house-made, and there's khao mok, oxtail soup, and salad khaek to order alongside.

faq.q: What's the difference between chicken and beef khao soi?
faq.a: Chicken khao soi has a more middle-of-the-road flavour and is easier to eat, usually served as a drumstick — good if it's your first time. Beef khao soi is more heavily braised, with a heavier broth that's more fragrant with spices. The shops known for their beef are Lamduan, Khao Soi Islam, and Lung Prakit at Kad Kom.
